newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. securities litigation bill expected soon.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. securities litigation bill expected soon.

text.p: Lawmakers are expected to propose legislation in the House of Representatives in the coming weeks that would stop securites class action suits from migrating to state courts, congressional aides and industry officials said on Tuesday.
The legislation is to be introduced by Democratic Rep. Anna Eshoo of California and Republican Rep. Rick White of Washington, congressional aides said.

The details of the measure, and how broad it will reach, were still not clear, the aides said. But its intent will be to stop litigators from using state courts to get round federal reforms passed by Congress in 1995.
"It just seems that we fixed this at one level but I think folks have found a way around the fix and that is through the state courts," an aide to White said.

The legislation has been sought by the Uniform Standards Coalition, a nationwide organization of high-tech companies, venture capitalists and others who are seeking congressional action to put an end to what they call frivolous lawsuits.
"What we've been doing is working with people on the Hill to put together some legislation that would create uniform standards," coalition executive director Mark Gitenstein said.
"The same set of rules ought to apply to federal litigation as to state litigation," he added.
The group, which spent millions to fight a ballot initiative in California it said would have undermined Congress' reforms, is now focusing its attention on Washington.

The hi-tech industry coalition claims that a small group of lawyers that specializes in securities class action suits has evaded the 1995 reforms by shifting cases to state courts, where the qualifying standards are lower.
The group says this is a costly and risky development for startup companies that want to avoid litigation.
"We're trying to fill that loophole, nothing more nothing less," Gitenstein said.
But their concerns, which have been taken up by some 60 House Democrats, including Eshoo, have received a lukewarm response from the White House.
"The new regime put in place by the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act is still in its infancy," President Clinton wrote in an April 25 letter to Eshoo.
That was the same message delivered by the Securities and Exchange Commission in its recent study of the law.
"My Administration will be reviewing the SEC study and other reports and data to assess the need for further action," Clinton wrote.

The controversial securities litigation reform, which was passed over a presidential veto in late 1995, is designed to reduce the amount of meritless cases in federal courts by, among other things, raising the qualifying standards.
Those opposed to the reform include consumer groups, which have cautioned that the new standards leave investors with little legal recourse.
"It will leave a lot of investors with little protection," warned Betsy Dotson, assistant director and legislative counsel for the Government Finance Officers Association's federal liaison center.
Dotson said the latest shift to state courts is "good lawyering."

"A lot of the states have longer statutes. There are things that make it easier for investors not only to get into court," Dotson said. "Not all cases that investors bring have merit, but they are not all frivolous either."
But Michael Timmeny, vice president for domestic policy for the American Electronics Association warned that companies, despite Congress' efforts, are still exposed to the costly lawsuits.
"We know first hand when these companies get sued, the Hell they go through," Timmeny said, adding that these companies usually settle to keep legal costs down.

Both he and Gitenstein warned that the move of securities class actions to state courts is even more risky for companies. "You cannot go into the capital markest and have 50 different rules apply," Gitenstein said.
